newsitem.title: UK: TEARFUL SEGERS DENIES HE THREW MATCH.
newsitem.headline: TEARFUL SEGERS DENIES HE THREW MATCH.

text.p: A tearful Hans Segers denied on Tuesday he had thrown a crucial soccer match between Everton and his side Wimbledon in 1994 and said football was his life-blood from morning until night.
Under cross examination the Dutch-born goalkeeper, charged with fixing matches for an Asian betting syndicate, admitted he had evaded income tax payments and lied to police.

But he denied a charge of conspiring to fix English premier league matches, saying he had never thrown a match in his life. Segers is charged with two other soccer players and a Malaysian businessman with trying to rig matches, charges they all deny.

The court in the southern English town of Winchester where Segers is standing trial was shown video evidence of the Everton versus Wimbledon match of May 7 1994 -- the last match of the 1993-94 season.
Wimbledon, with Segers playing in goal, lost 3-2 after taking a 2-0 lead. The result meant Everton retained their premier league status and another club, Sheffield United, were relegated.
Segers, questioned by his lawyer Desmond Da Silva, commented on Everton's three goals as the jury watched the video highlights.
The first was a penalty. Segers dived to his left but the shot went into the net to his right.
"I tried to anticipate the shot," Segers, 35, explained. "At that time I just guessed the wrong side."
He said he could do little to save Everton's powerfully struck second goal and had been deceived by the bounce of the ball in the dramatic 81st minute third goal.

"The pitch at the end of the match is quite rough," he said. "It's all bits and bobs all over the place. He hit a shot, I dived and had it covered all the way and it just hit a divot and popped up and changed direction."
Asked if he had ever tried to illegally influence the outcome of a soccer match, Segers said: "I've never thrown a match, I've never been asked to throw a match."

"At the time the article came out (in which the allegations became public in November 1994) I was really worried. I thought everything was going to be taken away from me, my livelihood... Football was everything I've got. I wake up with football and I go to bed with football.
His voice quaking with emotion, Segers admitted he had lied to police after his arrest in 1995.
"I'm sorry for that, I'm sorry I've done that, It's been really hard, really hard," he said, wiping a tear from his eye.
Later, chief prosecutor David Calvert Smith poured scorn on Segers' video defence.
"Now that we've seen that (third) goal, the divot theory doesn't stand up, does it?" he said.

In reply, Segers asked for the incident to be replayed in slow motion. This was done, and Segers stepped out of the witness box and stood by the TV screen, pointing out the rough ground in the penalty area where he stood.
Calvert Smith then moved on to the question of Segers' income tax evasion.
"You have lied about your income, you now tell us, to the income tax people," he said.
"I didn't lie. I just didn't tell them everything," Segers replied. "It was very foolish of me."
